knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>")
# RSiena writes report files to the working directory; keep them out of the site.
knitr::opts_knit$set(root.dir = tempdir())

This article continues from [Getting started](getting-started.html).
It is based on the scripts `Rscript03SienaRunModel.R` and
`RscriptOnestep.R` by Tom Snijders, with earlier contributions from
Robin Gauthier, Ruth Ripley, Johan Koskinen, and Paulina Preciado.

## Data and a first model

We use the `s50` data again, with friendship as the dependent network,
smoking at wave 1 as a constant covariate,
and alcohol use as a changing covariate.

```{r data, message = FALSE}
library(RSiena)
friendship <- as_dependent_rsiena(array(c(s501, s502, s503),
                                        dim = c(50, 50, 3)))
smoke1  <- as_covariate_rsiena(s50s[, 1])
alcohol <- as_covariate_rsiena(s50a)
mydata  <- make_data_rsiena(friendship, smoke1, alcohol)
```

The first model has transitivity, outdegree activity,
three effects of alcohol, and smoking similarity:

```{r model1}
myeff <- make_specification(mydata)
myeff <- set_effect(myeff, list(transTrip, outAct), verbose = FALSE)
myeff <- set_effect(myeff, list(egoX, altX, simX), covar1 = "alcohol",
                    verbose = FALSE)
myeff <- set_effect(myeff, simX, covar1 = "smoke1", verbose = FALSE)
myalgo <- set_algorithm_saom(seed = 1293)
ans <- siena(mydata, effects = myeff, control_algo = myalgo, batch = TRUE)
ans
```

## Reading the results

The **convergence t-ratio** in the last column checks the convergence
of the algorithm; it is not a test of the effect.
All convergence t-ratios should be less than 0.1 in absolute value,
and the overall maximum convergence ratio should be less than 0.25
(see Section 7.2 of the manual).

The results object holds, among other things,
the estimates, their standard errors, and their covariance matrix:

```{r components}
ans$theta
ans$se
```

`summary(ans)` gives a longer summary.
To make a table for a paper, use `siena_table(ans, type = "html")`
(or `type = "tex"`), which writes a file to the working directory.

The estimation simulates the network evolution,
so two runs give slightly different results.
For results that you report, set `n3` (the number of iterations in phase 3)
in `set_algorithm_saom()` to a larger value than the default 1000,
for example `n3 = 5000`, and set `seed` for reproducible results.

## Choosing the effects of an actor variable

How can you choose the effects of an actor variable such as alcohol use?
Snijders and Lomi (2019) propose to start from five effects,
and to interpret them together with a *selection table*.

> Snijders, T.A.B. and Lomi, A. (2019).
> Beyond homophily: Incorporating actor variables in statistical network models.
> *Network Science*, 7, 1–19.
> <https://doi.org/10.1017/nws.2018.30>

```{r five}
myeff2 <- make_specification(mydata)
myeff2 <- set_effect(myeff2, list(transTrip, outAct), verbose = FALSE)
myeff2 <- set_effect(myeff2, list(egoX, altX, egoSqX, egoXaltX, diffSqX),
                     covar1 = "alcohol", verbose = FALSE)
myeff2 <- set_effect(myeff2, simX, covar1 = "smoke1", verbose = FALSE)
ans2 <- siena(mydata, effects = myeff2, control_algo = myalgo, batch = TRUE)
ans2
```

It is almost impossible to interpret five parameters one by one.
The selection table gives, for each combination of the alcohol use
of ego (rows) and alter (columns), the total contribution of the
five alcohol effects to the evaluation function:

```{r seltable}
(table.alcohol <- interpret_selection(ans2, mydata, "friendship", "alcohol"))
```

The [autograph](https://stocnet.github.io/autograph/) package plots it.
There is one curve for each value of ego's alcohol use;
the horizontal axis gives alter's alcohol use.

```{r selplot, message = FALSE, fig.width = 7, fig.height = 4.5}
library(autograph)
plot(table.alcohol)
```

If the top of each curve is near ego's own value, this shows homophily.
Differences in the height of the curves
show how the tendency to have friends depends on ego's alcohol use.

### Backward selection

The model can then be made simpler, one effect at a time.
Remove the effect with the smallest absolute t-statistic,
but keep the lower-order effects of an interaction that stays in the model.
Here we remove `egoXaltX`, and then `altX`:

```{r backward}
myeff3 <- set_effect(myeff2, list(egoXaltX, altX), covar1 = "alcohol",
                     include = FALSE, verbose = FALSE)
ans3 <- siena(mydata, effects = myeff3, control_algo = myalgo, batch = TRUE)
ans3
```

```{r selplot3, fig.width = 7, fig.height = 4.5}
plot(interpret_selection(ans3, mydata, "friendship", "alcohol"))
```

Section 14.3 of the manual explains selection tables in more detail.

## Better convergence

If the convergence is not good enough,
continue from the previous results with `prevAns`.
The estimates in the previous results are then the starting values,
and phase 1 of the algorithm is skipped.
You can use `prevAns` if the specification is the same,
or if effects were only added.
If effects were dropped, start again without `prevAns`
(or use `update_theta()` to set the starting values).

For precise final results, continue with a long phase 2 subphase
and a long phase 3:

```{r precise}
algo1 <- set_algorithm_saom(nsub = 1, n2start = 2000, n3 = 5000, seed = 99)
ans <- siena(mydata, effects = myeff, control_algo = algo1,
             prevAns = ans, batch = TRUE)
ans$tconv.max
```

Section 7.3 of the manual gives more advice about convergence
and the settings of the algorithm.

## Testing effects

RSiena has three types of test.

### t-type tests of one parameter

Divide the estimate by its standard error.
`test_parameter()` gives the test.
For alcohol similarity:

```{r ttest}
alcsim <- which(ans$effects$shortName == "simX" &
                ans$effects$interaction1 == "alcohol")
test_parameter(ans, tested = alcsim)
```

A one-sided test is appropriate when the direction of the effect
was expected in advance; then divide the two-sided p-value by 2.

### Tests of several parameters

`test_parameter()` with several parameters gives a joint Wald-type test.
Compare the three alcohol effects in the first model
with the three alcohol effects in the model from the backward selection:

```{r wald}
alc  <- which(ans$effects$interaction1 == "alcohol")
alc3 <- which(ans3$effects$interaction1 == "alcohol")
test_parameter(ans, tested = alc)
test_parameter(ans3, tested = alc3)
```

### Score tests

A score test tests an effect without estimating it.
Include the effect, fix it at 0, and mark it to be tested.
Here we test the effect of indegree popularity:

```{r score}
myeff <- set_effect(myeff, inPop, fix = TRUE, test = TRUE, verbose = FALSE)
ans4 <- siena(mydata, effects = myeff, control_algo = myalgo,
              prevAns = ans, batch = TRUE)
inpop <- which(ans4$effects$shortName == "inPop")
test_parameter(ans4, tested = inpop, method = "score")
```

See `?test_parameter` for more options.

## Time heterogeneity

Are the parameters the same in the two periods?
`test_time()` applies a score test for each effect
and each period.

> Lospinoso, J.A., Schweinberger, M., Snijders, T.A.B. and Ripley, R.M. (2011).
> Assessing and accounting for time heterogeneity in stochastic actor oriented models.
> *Advances in Data Analysis and Classification*, 5, 147–176.
> <https://doi.org/10.1007/s11634-010-0076-1>

```{r timetest}
tt <- test_time(ans)
summary(tt)
```

If the overall test is significant, the effect-wise and period-wise
results show where the heterogeneity is.
`includeTimeDummy()` then adds parameters for the separate periods.

## Summary of the code

```{r summary, eval = FALSE}
library(RSiena)
friendship <- as_dependent_rsiena(array(c(s501, s502, s503),
                                        dim = c(50, 50, 3)))
smoke1  <- as_covariate_rsiena(s50s[, 1])
alcohol <- as_covariate_rsiena(s50a)
mydata  <- make_data_rsiena(friendship, smoke1, alcohol)
write_report(mydata)
myeff <- make_specification(mydata)
myeff <- set_effect(myeff, list(transTrip, outAct))
myeff <- set_effect(myeff, list(egoX, altX, simX), covar1 = "alcohol")
myeff <- set_effect(myeff, simX, covar1 = "smoke1")
ans <- siena(mydata, effects = myeff, batch = TRUE)
ans
```
